newsitem.title: USA: Family says fighter pilot died in Arizona jet crash.
newsitem.headline: Family says fighter pilot died in Arizona jet crash.

text.p: The pilot of an A-10 fighter aircraft that went down during a training mission in Arizona was killed in the crash, the pilot's family said on Wednesday.

The Air Force did not publicly announce that Capt. Amy Lynn Svoboda had died, but her family said they were informed that remains found in the wreckage were identified as belonging to the 29-year-old woman.
"Since the first time she expressed her desire to fly for the Air Force we have been excited for and proud of her accomplishments," said a family statement.

"She was a beautiful girl who loved life and flying and was very proud to serve her country as one of the Air Force's first woman fighter pilots. She was taken from us far too soon even though she died courageously doing what she loved."

Officials at Davis-Monthan Air Force base in Arizona earlier refused to confirm Svoboda died in the crash of her single-seater on a routine training mission on Tuesday at the Barry Goldwater Training Range in southwest Arizona.

The Air Force said the A-10, designed to destroy tanks and other armor, was carrying a variety of practice weapons, including six 25-pound training bombs that emit smoke and a small flash. Authorities said these units have the same ballistic characteristics as larger, live ordnance.
Also on board were six 2.75-inch air-to-ground rockets and 570 rounds of 33mm practice rounds for a Gatling gun. Additionally, the aircraft was carrying an AIM-9 practice air-to-air missle.
Svoboda was assigned to the 355th fighter wing and had been at Davis-Monthan for about a year, Air Force officials said.

She graduated from the Air Force Academy in 1989 and trained at Reese Air Force Base in Texas. She remained there as a T-37 instructor pilot until 1996 when she transferred to Davis-Monthan for A-10 training where she was certified as a combat-ready pilot.
Tech Sgt. Dan Carpenter said Svoboda was an experienced fighter jet pilot having logged 1,400 hours. She was the No. 2 training officer in her squadron.
The jet was part of a two-aircraft mission. The other plane was not involved in the accident.

The crash was the second involving an A-10 from Davis-Monthan in almost two months. In April, Capt. Craig Button, 32, inexplicably left his four-aircraft formation and veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles away (1360 km) from a training exercise.
The formation was en route to the Barry Goldwater Training Range at the time.
Button's plane crashed into a snow-covered mountain peak and it was more than three weeks before a rescue team was able to recover his body.
